extracted.intended_audience: readers of The New Yorker; literary-humor enthusiasts and magazine editors/curators
extracted.subtask_description: Selecting and presenting short-form literary humor for a magazine readership, emphasizing a range of forms and tones from parody to cartoons while preserving editorial standards. Useful for editors, curators, and writers aiming to place or frame humor in a literary magazine context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include wit and satire but be more than simply 'a jester'
rubrics_metrics.description: Harold Ross stated in the magazine’s prospectus that, although The New Yorker might include wit and satire, it would be more than simply “a jester.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor may be present, but pieces should have substance or literary/journalistic weight beyond mere joking; they should fit within the magazine’s broader intellectual or investigative remit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor of all shapes and sizes (variety of forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the early years of The New Yorker, humor of all shapes and sizes filled the magazine—sketches, parodies, satirical Comments and Fiction, and more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curate or publish a range of formal types (sketches, parodies, satirical essays, short fiction, Shouts & Murmurs, cartoons) rather than privileging a single format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained playfulness and whimsy as a through line
rubrics_metrics.description: The magazine has retained a lively through line of playfulness and whimsy, in the form of Shouts & Murmurs and cartoons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a recognizable tonal thread (playfulness/whimsy) across different pieces so humor contributes to the publication’s character and reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective parody and dry wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Nora Ephron’s parody of a newspaper column lends her dry wit — e.g., ‘Nobody in this column ever has a name!’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accurate mimicry of a target form or voice and incisive, economical observations; parodies succeed when they reveal recognizable habits of the thing being lampooned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evocative, concise inventorying or detail for humor
rubrics_metrics.description: F. Scott Fitzgerald chronicles stages of his life by cherished vintage: ‘1928: The Pouilly with Bouillabaisse at Prunier’s in a time of discouragement.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific, well-chosen details (lists, vintage items, images) can compress character and elicit gentle irony or nostalgia that reads as humorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdist reimagining of the mundane
rubrics_metrics.description: Ian Frazier imagines how Samuel Beckett might have depicted air travel (LGA—ORD), turning an everyday experience into an absurdist conceit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place ordinary situations in an unexpected voice or frame; recontextualization and incongruity generate comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sharp monologue and punchline economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Dorothy Parker’s ‘Just a Little One’ demonstrates monologue that begins breezily and devolves into sharply timed lines: ‘You know what I like about this place? It’s got atmosphere...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economy of language, voice consistency, and well-timed punchlines or ironic reversals are key to short comic monologues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception-versus-reality comedic contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: James Thurber’s ‘The Secret Life of Walter Mitty’ presents a man who perceives his journey as more wondrous than it actually is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor can be generated by the gap between a character’s inner fantasies and external reality; exploit contrast and escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic exploration of existential or psychological themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Steve Martin’s ‘Closure’ pursues an intense longing for a sense of completion, using irony and self-reflection for comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use irony, self-awareness, or exaggerated introspection to make deeper human longings into a source of humor without undercutting emotional resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provocation or frankness as satirical device
rubrics_metrics.description: Upton Sinclair’s ‘How to Be Obscene’ suggests dealing ‘the facts of life frankly and honestly’ to create a stir, noting you don’t have to write anything really harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provocative or candid treatment of taboo subjects can function as satire; the aim can be to provoke thought or controversy rather than to shock gratuitously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor’s reader effect: offer enjoyment and relief
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor expresses hope that these pieces offer enjoyment, and a bit of relief, to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting or writing humor for a general readership, consider the emotional payoff — laughter, pleasure, and relief — as an explicit goal of the piece.
